fixes.why: The hub's words are the Hebrew רחם family and the Greek ἔλεος family, yet two of its seven key verses, the two a reader will look for first, are חֶסֶד in the Hebrew, the word the Berean usually prints 'loving devotion'. As shown they sit among the key verses as if they were the hub's own words and in no row, and a reader who clicks to see where they belong finds nothing. That is an unflagged gap between what the page implies (these verses are about this word) and what is true. Putting them in a row would break rule 4; leaving them unmarked is the quieter version of the same fault.
fixes.fix: Keep them as key verses (the card does name them) but mark them as the memory rule says: an asterisk at 'mercy' in each verse and beside it one sentence, 'In the Hebrew this is חֶסֶד, usually “loving devotion” in the Berean; it is not the word the rows below are built on. See Love, where חֶסֶד is set out.' Link to the love hub's חֶסֶד entry (168 uses in love.json's others). Do not add either verse to any row, and do not call them 'also mercy'. Mic 6:8 also deserves the pointer because 'justice, mercy' is the verse people come for: say so once, plainly, rather than let the rows imply the text has no such pairing.

fixes.row: Other words translated “mercy”, “compassion” and “pity” (the חֶסֶד entry)
fixes.why: The others list shows חֶסֶד with 2 verses (1 Kgs 20:31, Ps 23:6), which tells a reader the word is rarely rendered mercy and omits the two verses where it is the most quoted. The builder reads MACULA's gloss, not the Berean's printed word, so the count is an artifact. A reader who adds up the page will be misled in both directions: the entry understates, and the key verses contradict it.
fixes.fix: Until the builder can match the Berean's printed word, add a note to that entry: 'The Berean prints “mercy” for חֶסֶד in a few verses: here, and Hos 6:6 and Mic 6:8, the key verses above. Everywhere else it prints “loving devotion” (see Love).' Or add Hos 6:6 and Mic 6:8 to that entry's verses by hand.

fixes.why: The row carries only Matthew's two quotations, filed under Hosea's words, and Hosea 6:6 itself is not in the row or pointed to; the Hebrew Scriptures should be heard first. The note's closing 'They are two words' can also be read by a reader with a high view of Scripture as a correction of Jesus or Matthew, which the text does not say (Matthew's Greek is how the quotation reads in Greek).
fixes.fix: Open the note with a link to Hos 6:6: 'Hosea 6:6, in the Hebrew: חֶסֶד, printed “mercy” there and usually “loving devotion” (see Love). Jesus quotes it in Matthew, where the Greek word is ἔλεος.' Drop 'They are two words' or change it to 'The hub's rows are built on the Greek and the Hebrew רחם words; Hosea's word is set out under Love.' Do not suggest a mismatch.

fixes.why: The label is 1 Pet 2:10's past tense. Prov 28:13 is a future conditional ('whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy'), not mercy received, and it is the first example a reader sees, so an Old Testament proverb is led under a New Testament heading it does not say. It also puts a condition up front, and the row has no note: with 1 Tim 1:13 ('because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy') the row quietly lays out reasons mercy was given, and Christian traditions part on what mercy waits on. The 'Compassion, and forgiveness' row already holds exactly this question (Isa 55:7) and carries the no-side note.
fixes.fix: Move Prov 28:13 to 'Compassion, and forgiveness', next to Isa 55:7, where the note applies, and put 1 Pet 2:10 first in this row. Add to this row: 'Each verse gives its own reason, or none; the page takes no side on what mercy depends on.'

fixes.why: The row's note describes it as the openings of the letters and Gal 6:16, and the label reads as a blessing. Jer 16:5 (the fifth verse in the list) is the opposite: 'I have removed from this people My peace, My loving devotion, and My compassion.' An Old Testament verse of withdrawal sits inside a New Testament greeting formula. It is a real pairing in the text, but the label says only the greeting.
fixes.fix: Take Jer 16:5 out of this row (it is already in 'Mercy shown, and no mercy shown' and 'Compassion beside חֶסֶד'). If it stays, relabel the row 'Mercy and peace, given and taken away' and extend the note: 'Jer 16:5 is the LORD taking them away.'

fixes.row: No compassion, no mercy, no pity
fixes.why: Zech 1:12 is the angel's question 'How long ... will You withhold mercy?', a plea put to the LORD, and in v. 16 He returns 'with mercy'. Placed beside 'He has no compassion' it can be read as a statement that He withholds it. The row has no note to say which verses state and which ask.
fixes.fix: Add a note to the row: 'Zech 1:12 is a question put to the LORD, “How long?”; the verses of this row are said of the LORD, of the enemy He raises, or asked of Him.' Alternatively move Zech 1:12 to 'Asking for mercy' (it already appears in 'Beside justice, judgment and anger').

fixes.why: The label says 'me' but four of the eleven say 'us' or 'my son', which the first examples show; and the row is wholly Gospel, so a reader sees no Hebrew cry for mercy. The best-known one, Ps 51:1 'Have mercy on me, O God', is a different Hebrew word (חָנַן) and is shown only under Other words (and as a hidden member of 'Asking for mercy' by the noun), so the Hebrew Scriptures are not heard first on the cry.
fixes.fix: Relabel “Have mercy on me, on us”, or add a note: 'The cry in the Gospels, to Jesus and from the rich man to Abraham. The Hebrew cry of Ps 51:1 is another word, חָנַן, set out under Other words.' Do not add Ps 51:1 here.

fixes.why: Rom 9:23 ('the vessels of His mercy, whom He prepared in advance for glory') is the other half of Rom 9:15-18, which carries the no-side note in the verb tab. Here it sits in an unlabelled catch-all with no note, away from the passage it belongs to, and a reader who sees only this row takes it as a plain statement with the note's protection missing. The same holds for Rom 11:31 and the verb row 'Mercy through disobedience'.
fixes.fix: Add a note to this catch-all: 'Rom 9:23 belongs with Rom 9:15-18 (the verb row “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy”) and Rom 11:31 with Rom 11:30-32; where Christian traditions part on those passages, the page takes no side.'

worker_points.point: 1. 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy' (Exod 33:19, Rom 9:15, 9:16, 9:18): does grouping 9:16 with the other three tilt?
worker_points.why: Exod 33:19 comes first, so the Hebrew Scriptures lead; the verses are quoted whole (9:18 includes both mercy and hardening) and the no-side note sits on the row. The tilt risk is in the neighbour, Rom 9:23, which has no note (see fixes).

worker_points.point: 2. Mercy through disobedience (Rom 11:30-32) and universalist/particularist readers
worker_points.why: Three consecutive verses, kept whole, no-side note. The label is Paul's phrase. Rabbi: Israel is 'they' in the verses themselves; nothing is added.

worker_points.point: 3. Not our deeds, but His mercy (Dan 9:18, Titus 3:5); fold into 'Asking for mercy'?
worker_points.why: Keep the row: Dan 9:18 comes first and fits it, and Titus 3:5 earns its own note (washing of new birth; mercy and works). Folding would lose the OT voice of the same thought.

worker_points.point: 4. Mercy and peace (Gal 6:16 'the Israel of God')
worker_points.why: The no-side note is adequate and the rabbi may accept it. The row itself needs the Jer 16:5 fix.

worker_points.point: 5. Compassion, and forgiveness: does forgiveness wait on repentance?
worker_points.why: The note is right. Prov 28:13 should join this row (see the 'received mercy' fix) so that the question and its note stay together.

Handled by hand with notes that name the text's own word and decline to choose. Jude 21 names Christ and is correctly kept in the same row with that statement. Divine persons are not inferred anywhere.

worker_points.point: 7. Divine persons: LORD rows that name Him only by address ('You': Ps 102:13, Hos 14:3, Mic 7:19) or by His speech ('I': Isa 60:10, Jer 12:15, Hos 2:23); Isa 49:10 'He' out; Heb 2:17 'He'
worker_points.why: 'You' and 'I' are the text naming Him through speech or address in the passage, and it is by hand, not a rule. Isa 49:10 stays out, as it should. Heb 2:17 stands in its own one-verse row with a hand note (Heb 2:9 names Jesus) and its label says only what the verse says.

worker_points.point: 8. Hard verses stay (Lam 4:10, Hos 1:6, the no-compassion row)
worker_points.why: They belong: they are the text, they are the shadow the Hosea reversal and Jas 2:13 rest on, and the rabbi and the secular reader would count their absence as a softening. Zech 1:12 alone is mis-set (see fixes).

worker_points.point: 9. Hos 6:6 / Mic 6:8 as key verses, חֶסֶד not in rows
worker_points.why: Keeping them out of the rows is right (rule 4), but the hub names them as key verses with nothing to say so, and the others list under-reports חֶסֶד. See the first two fixes; the note on the Matthew row should be moved to the verses themselves and the About text.

worker_points.point: 10. Works of mercy / alms (ἐλεημοσύνη) not included
worker_points.why: The Berean prints 'alms', so it is a different word and the omission is honest; the text's own mercy-to-others verses are in the 'Show mercy to others' row. Luke 6:36 (be merciful as your Father) is in another word (see missing). No false claim is made.
Rule 4: a different word, listed apart with 12 verses, never placed at the head. Rule 3 also supports it.

worker_points.point: 12. ἱλάσκομαι, ἵλεως and חנן under others
worker_points.why: Listed apart with verses only, no claim about propitiation. The reader is not told they equal mercy.

missing.what: The Psalmists' 'cry/plea/appeal for mercy' (תַּחֲנוּן, Hebrew 'supplication', which the Berean prints with 'mercy'): about eight verses of the Hebrew Scriptures' own asking, absent from 'Asking for mercy' and from Other words (which shows only Dan 9:3 and Jer 31:9). Without them the Old Testament is thin exactly where the New Testament has a row of its own, 'Have mercy on me'. They are another word and must be shown apart, not merged.

The text's own reversal of Hosea's 'No Compassion' (Hos 1:6, 2:23) in 1 Pet 2:10 is stated only in the spec's _why. A reader of the hub sees the verses in three separate rows with nothing linking them; a cross-note on 1 Pet 2:10 (and on Hos 2:23) would let the text speak for itself.

'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful' (οἰκτίρμων) and 'the Lord is full of compassion and mercy' (πολύσπλαγχνος, the echo of Exod 34:6) are in Other words but not signposted from 'Show mercy to others' or from the adjective row, so a reader of those rows would think the New Testament has no such command or statement.

summary: The hub is faithful to the text: it keeps the Hebrew and Greek words together without equating either with חֶסֶד, handles the divine persons by hand, and leaves the hard verses in. It ships after the key verses Hos 6:6 and Mic 6:8 are honestly marked as חֶסֶד, the others-list count for חֶסֶד is corrected, and four small misfits (Prov 28:13, Jer 16:5, Zech 1:12, the 'Have mercy on me' label) plus two missing notes are repaired.
